kicker: Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing · update report
title: Steadier frames, a living soundscape and 34 scientists
lede: The game no longer stalls the first time something comes into view, no longer draws the whole scene twice when the observatory is in sight, leaves out what is too small to see, sounds like the place you are in, and has 34 busts of scientists to find.

sections.title: What you asked for, and where it stands
sections.html:
Every point in your message, in the order you wrote it. The first seven repeat your previous message: the iPhone fixes went out in commit 524a864 and the climbing, Tesla and science work in c73b7cd, and this round adds to two of them. The last three are new.

#You askedWhat changedStatus
1On iPhone in landscape the RUN button sits in the small mapOn short screens RUN sits beside the small map, not on it (since 524a864, checked at 15 screen sizes last round). This round the Journal gained a tab, and the layout was checked again at eleven sizes, from an iPhone SE to a desktop screen, with nothing overlapping.Done, not tested on a real iPhone
2The voice that says "fish on" sounds too robotic: a more natural voiceThe game already picks the most natural voice the phone has (Enhanced and Premium first, the novelty voices never). A web page can only use the voices installed on the phone, and an iPhone ships with compact ones. New: the first time the announcer speaks with a compact voice on an iPhone, iPad or Mac, a note says how to download a natural one for free (Settings, Accessibility, Spoken Content, Voices, English, one marked Enhanced or Premium) and pick it in the game under Settings, Voice.Done, not tested on a real iPhone
3The buttons in the top right do nothing when tappedThey answer the touch itself since 524a864; unchanged.Done, not tested on a real iPhone
4Very laggy at timesThree causes found and fixed: every kind of thing is now drawn once behind the loading bar, so nothing stalls the first time it comes into view; a glass bubble 24 cm across that made the whole scene draw twice whenever the observatory was in view is plain glass; parts too small to see are left out. See Steady frames.Done
5Rock climbing that fits the themeThe Granite Tors, four routes (last round).Done
6A statue of Nikola TeslaThe Tesla Memorial at Bear Falls (last round). Its statue is now carved by the same three.js-free sculptor as the new busts.Done
7General science objectives in the quests23 last round; now 25, with two for the new busts in a sixth field, the people of science.Done
8The sound from the environment needs a lot of improvementRebuilt: wind tied to the gusts you see, rivers with their babble, the falls, waves breaking, rain, drips, thunder, mosquitoes, birds singing as birds do, footsteps for every ground, all placed in space with a reverb. See The sound of the place, with recordings to listen to.Done
9Optimise for a stable frame rate without sacrificing graphics qualityThe fixes in row 4, none of which changes how anything looks (checked picture against picture), plus less garbage for the phone to clear up and no shader error checks in the release build.Done
10A lot of small statues of famous scientists, wherever they fit34 busts in bronze, dark bronze and marble on granite plinths, each by a place their work belongs to, each with a plaque to read. See 34 scientists.Done

sections.title: Steady frames
sections.html:
"Laggy at times" is the feel of single long frames: the game runs smoothly, then stops for a moment. To find them, every frame of a fixed tour was timed (turning round at Hotrod Landing, walking into the forest, driving the Coast Road, Bear Falls with the Tesla Memorial, the observatory at night), each frame split into the game's own work, the world's update and the drawing, and everything drawn was counted. Three causes stood out. None of the fixes changes the picture.

Nothing is built for the first time during play

Every kind of surface (bark in sunlight, a fish's scales, glass, the hands on the rod) is drawn by a small program on the graphics chip, a shader. Each one is built once, and on an iPhone Safari finishes building it, through Apple's Metal, only when it first draws something. The old build asked for the shaders while loading, but that left the last part of the work for the first time each thing came into view, and the hands were prepared without the sky's reflections they are drawn with, so theirs were built again the moment play began. Those were the stops: when you started, at the first look into the forest, at the first fish.

The loading bar now has a last step, Preparing the view. The game switches on everything that could appear (hidden things, empty fish schools, things too far away or behind the camera), lets the browser build the shaders side by side in the background where it can (three.js's compileAsync, which uses the browser's parallel shader compiling where there is one), then draws all of it once into a single pixel, so the driver finishes its part behind the loading bar. Then everything is put back as it was.

Test browser, 320 by 180Loading, to the titlePressing New gameFirst frame of playSecond frameShaders built after loading
Before15 s257 ms12.2 s27 ms3
After16 s517 ms62 ms19 ms0

The test browser builds shaders in software and slowly, so its seconds are far longer than a phone's; what carries over is where the wait falls: behind the loading bar now, in play before. Pressing New game took 0.34 to 0.52 s in three runs of this build: about 0.06 s of it is the new sound starting, most of the rest is dressing the player's arms, as before, and it varies from run to run.

One more turned up in the final tests: the sun rays are drawn only when the sun is in view, so the warm-up, looking elsewhere, never built their shader, and the first look toward the sun stopped the game (for 8 to 31 seconds in the test browser, which builds shaders slowly in software). The warm-up now draws the rays whichever way it looks, and the full tour, turning a whole circle in the sun at Hotrod Landing, builds no shader at all.

The observatory no longer doubles the drawing

The all-sky camera on the observatory's deck sits under a glass bubble 24 cm across. Its glass was three.js's physical glass that bends what is behind it (transmission). For that one material three.js draws every solid thing in view a second time, into a picture of its own, every frame the bubble is inside the camera's view, however small or far away, even behind a hill: three.js does not know what hides what. The bubble is now clear glass with the same shine; at its size the bending could not be seen. Measured on its own, this took the drive along the Coast Road from 844 draw calls a frame to 487, and from 2.7 to 1.6 million triangles.

Parts too small to see are left out

The buildings, the observatory, the cars, the Tesla Memorial, the boat, the busts and the props are made of many small parts: hinges, bolts, cups, rivets, letters. Far away, many of them cover less than a pixel, yet each still costs a draw call and a place in the shadows. Each part is now measured against the screen (a quarter of them each frame, all of them after a jump), left out below one pixel across and brought back above one and a quarter, before it can be seen. The two pictures of each view below were drawn with and without leaving parts out, at the same moment, and compared pixel by pixel.

View (640 by 360)Small parts left outDraw calls withoutDraw calls withPixels that differLargest difference (of 255)
The Coast Road164 of 2464743520 of 230,4000
Hotrod Landing133 of 2462362340 of 230,4000

Smaller things

  • No shader error checks in the release build. After building each shader, three.js asks the driver for its error log, which makes the game wait for the build instead of letting it finish in the background. The check stays on while developing.
  • Less garbage. A phone stops now and then to clear away objects the game no longer uses. The hands' lighting and the animals' herding made new objects every frame; they now reuse their own.
  • Heavy work out of the frame. The busts are sculpted by background workers and the sounds baked in steps of a millisecond or two, so neither ever holds up a frame (see 34 scientists and the sound).

Measured along the tour

The tour is 90 frames in each of five places, stepped at a fixed sixtieth of a second, in the build before this round and in this one, with the same tool. The test browser draws in software, thousands of times slower than a phone's graphics chip, so the pixels themselves are skipped and everything else about drawing is timed: choosing what to draw, sorting, shadows, setting up each draw. Before each frame the software renderer is let catch up, outside the timing, so a frame never pays for work queued before it. That makes the draw calls and triangles the solid numbers here, and the times a guide to the processor's share. The worst frame is the one to watch: a stall shows there.

At this size drawing takes less time at every place, half on the Coast Road. The game's own share of the frame is 1 to 2 ms higher at the first two places: that is the sound being baked, about 0.4 s of work done a millisecond or two a frame, and the tour starts the moment loading ends. Played normally it is done within a few seconds of the title showing; at the later places, with it done, the game's share is within 0.3 ms of the old build's. This build's worst frame at each place is, but for one, the first frame after the jump there, at most 39 ms at this size and 43 ms at the phone's; among the old build's worst were waits for shaders, 130 ms in the forest at this size and over 12 seconds on the first frame of play.

At the phone's size drawing is quicker at four places of five and level in the forest, where the busts with their plinths and plaques add ten draws, most of them shadows, and leaving out small parts saves six; the Coast Road again shows the biggest gain.

sections.title: The sound of the place
sections.html:
Before, the world's sound was six mono noise loops through simple filters (wind, river, sea, rain, the falls), a random high beep standing in for every bird, and one footstep sound per surface. Now it is built in layers, all still synthesised in the game (no sound files), changing with where you are, the weather and the hour.

Beds that loop under everything

  • Wind in two bands, a low rush and a higher whoosh, wide in stereo. Its gusts are the same gusts that roll across the grass and bend the trees round you: the game works out the visual gust at your position and turns it into sound, so a gust you see sweeping toward you arrives in your ears as it reaches you. Under the trees the wind drops and the leaves take over; on the open tundra, the shore and high ground it is stronger, with a whistle in the gusts.
  • Leaves and needles rustling, made of thousands of tiny bursts, louder in the gusts, only where the forest is thick.
  • The river in three layers: a low roar, the rush of moving water, and its babble, which is what you mostly hear of running water: air bubbles, each ringing briefly at a pitch set by its size, rising as it nears the surface (the bubble resonance Marcel Minnaert described in 1933). Seventy bubbles a second, baked into a loop. The river sounds from the river's side of you, and the babble only close to it.
  • Bear Falls: a heavy roar and a deep rumble, from the falls' side of you.
  • The sea: a slow wash, from the sea's side of you.
  • Rain: a hiss, a patter of hundreds of drops a second, louder on the car's roof, and drips from the trees that go on after the rain stops while the forest is wet.

Things that happen

  • Waves breaking on the shore every four to ten seconds, more often the nearer you are: the surge building, the crash, and the backwash drawing the pebbles down with a hiss.
  • Water lapping at a lake's shore and at the river's edge.
  • Thunder rolling in the distance in a downpour, two or three rolls dying away, each storm from its own direction.
  • Mosquitoes whining round your head on Mosquito Flats, now in one ear, now the other, now right at it; not in wind or rain, and much fewer with bug dope on.
  • Bees going by in the meadows on warm days.
  • Wolves howling now and then at night from the hills round you, two or three voices, each its own pitch.

Birds, as birds sing

A few singers at a time, each on its own perch, singing its species' song over and over and then moving on, so a robin keeps singing from the same tree while you fish. Which species depends on the ground round you and how many on the hour: a dawn chorus, a quieter midday, an evening chorus, few in rain or a gale, and at night owls in the woods and loons on the lakes. Each song follows the bird's real pattern:

WhereBirdSong

ForestHermit thrushA clear level opening note, then a flute-like flourish above it, the next song at another pitch

Night, forestGreat horned owlHoo, h'hoo, hoo, hoo, low and soft
Night, lakesCommon loonThe wail, rising and falling across the water, or the quavering tremolo

Placed in space

Every sound from the world comes from its side, quieter and duller with distance (the air soaks up the highs), a little duller behind you, and partly through a reverb whose impulse response is synthesised too: thick under the trees, thin on the open tundra. Inside the car with the cockpit view the outside goes dull, and under water duller still.

Footsteps

Six variants for every kind of ground, never the same one twice running, left foot then right: grass, the forest floor's needles and twigs, rock, crunching snow, sand, gravel, the gravel road, spongy tundra, ice, sucking mud, hollow boards and splashing shallows.

Without hitches

The rich textures (stereo noise in three colours, the babble, the rain, the drips, the leaves, the woodpecker, the squirrel, 72 footsteps and the reverb) are baked in plain sample arrays from the title screen on, a millisecond or two a frame, in steps short enough not to show. Beds that are silent stop their loops after a few seconds, so they cost nothing; no more than ten placed sounds play at once.

Measured

Ten recordings, eight seconds each, of what comes out of the game's mix (after its compressor) at different places, hours and weathers. Loudness is the average level (RMS) in decibels below full scale; lows are under 300 Hz, mids 300 to 3,000 Hz, highs above. Where there are birds, rain or footsteps the mids and highs rise, as they should. The clips below are raised 6 dB for listening, all by the same amount; the table gives the game's own levels. Which birds sing is chosen afresh each time, so another take of the same place has other singers.

sections.title: Busts by the places their work belongs to
sections.html:
Thirty-four busts of scientists stand round Kenai Country on granite plinths, each by a place their work belongs to: the astronomers, and Ada Lovelace with the first computer program, at the Tundra Observatory; Ångström, Birkeland and Alfvén, who explained the aurora, on the tundra below it; Einstein by the Sun's sign of the solar system walk and Sagan by its Neptune; Faraday, Maxwell and Noether by the Tesla Memorial at Bear Falls; Hutton and Lehmann at the Granite Tors; Wegener, Arrhenius and Foote by Glacier Lake; Celsius and Mendeleev at Steaming Springs; Darwin and Franklin at Salmon Bend; Archimedes by Moose Lake; Fresnel and Ibn al-Haytham, who studied light, by Kachemak Light; Carson and Tharp, who studied the sea, above Halibut Pier; Curie, Linnaeus and Nobel round the Trading Post; Ross on Mosquito Flats; Anning at Shipwreck Cove and Maathai in the forest behind Ruben's cabin.

  • Each in their own likeness, sculpted from a description: a man's or a woman's face, young or old, the hair of their time (a periwig, a bun, a bob, a turban, a bonnet, a wild halo), the beard (moustache, side whiskers, pointed, full, long), glasses, and the clothes (a coat and cravat, a ruff, a falling band, a high-collared gown, a robe, a turtleneck, a dashiki). In bronze weathered green where the rain runs, dark bronze, or white marble with faint veins, the nose of the bronzes rubbed bright by visitors.
  • READ THE PLAQUE on the plinth's bronze plate: what they found, in two short paragraphs, and how it ties to the place (Darwin's salmon, Celsius's hot springs, Fresnel's lighthouse lens, Ross's mosquitoes, Linnaeus naming the fireweed round you).
  • The Journal's Scientists page keeps what you have read and says where each of the others stands. Two science objectives: read 10 plaques ($250) and all 34 ($600).
  • Placed where they fit: each bust has a spot found for it on dry, gentle ground, off the roads, clear of buildings, decks, parking, things to use and the other busts; the trees and grass round it are cleared.
  • No frame waits for them: the busts are sculpted by two background workers while the title is up (all 34 within about five seconds on the test machine), in a fine version for close up and a light one (about a fifth of the triangles) for beyond 22 m. The 34 plinths are one draw and the plaques another, all their lettering in one texture, and the busts too far away to cover a pixel are left out of the frame.

sections.title: What was run, and what it showed
sections.html:
Every check ran on this round's final build, in headless Chromium drawing in software (SwiftShader), or in Node for the parts that need no browser. The scripts are in the repository, in tools/ and tools/scenarios/.

ScriptWhat it doesResult
perf-tour.mjsTimes every frame of a fixed tour (five places, 90 frames each) in the build before this round and in this one, at 320 by 180 and at the size of an iPhone on its side; counts draw calls and triangles, and every shader built or waited for on the wayThe tables in Steady frames. Along the tour this build builds no shader and waits for none; the old one built the sun rays' at Hotrod Landing and waited for compiles there and in the forest

A fault in the test tools, found and fixed

The first full runs crashed: the test browser's page grew past 8 GB and was stopped. The cause was not the game. When the game starts on a computer it asks for pointer lock (the mouse steers the view), and the headless test browser then sends the locked pointer a steady stream of mouse events. While the slow software renderer holds the page for tens of seconds those events pile up, about 50 MB a second, in the page and in the browser. The previous build does exactly the same, a page held at the title (no pointer lock yet) does not, and releasing the pointer stops it. An iPhone never takes pointer lock. The test tools now run without it unless a scenario is about the pointer, and the runs that hold the page longest got much faster: the sound tour, which had slowed to one frame a second and crashed, now records all ten scenes in about two minutes.

The same digging showed that the old frame-time tour charged single frames for work the software renderer had queued before them (up to 25 s). The tour now lets it catch up before each frame, outside the timing; the old build was measured again the same way for the tables.

sections.title: What the review found, and what was fixed
sections.html:
A separate reviewer read every change of this round (code only, with small checks of the sculptor and the sound baker run on their own). Everything it confirmed is fixed and the checks below were run again on the fixed build.

FoundSeverityFix
The warm-up's undo hid about 80 of the 144 squares of ground after loading (holes to the sky until each square changed its detail level): the world update inside the warm-up made them visible, and putting back the hidden objects hid them again. The camera was also still at the middle of the map.HighThe world is brought up to date before anything is shown for the warm-up, with the title's camera placed first. After loading: 0 of 144 hidden.
After a phone takes the graphics context away and gives it back (in the background, short of memory), the busts would have stopped the game drawing: their arrays were let go once on the graphics chip, and three.js uploads everything again.MediumThe light copies keep their arrays (a few MB for all 34) and show at once; the fine ones are sculpted again by the worker.
The warm-up drew the whole view at full resolution, not one pixel: sizing the finish's buffers inside the draw reset the scissor.MediumThe buffers are sized before the scissor is set.
Animal calls through the new placed voices came out 15 to 27 dB quieter than before; wolves would hardly be heard.MediumLoud callers carry: full loudness out to 150 m for wolves, 120 m for loons, 50 m for eagles, 40 m for owls, 30 m for gulls and ravens, 600 m for thunder.
Water lapping was placed at sea level: silent at Glacier Lake, too quiet at Moose Lake.LowAt the water's own level.
The mosquitoes kept whining in menus and after quitting to the title.LowThey leave with the menu.
Thunder and some wolf howls were cut off before they ended, with a click.LowTheir sounds live as long as they last.
Changing the graphics quality could flash the view black for a frame or two.LowThe warm draw runs in a frame of its own, followed by the whole view.
About 10 MB of baked sound stayed in memory after becoming audio buffers.LowLet go once converted.
The better-voice note would show iPhone instructions on a Mac, and judged voices by name only.LowiPhones and iPads only (an iPad that calls itself a Mac counts), and the voice's identifier is checked too.
An unused file; a bust that cannot be sculpted would have broken every frame after it; a line in the climbing code that did nothing.SmallRemoved; caught (the bust stays unmade); reverted.

Checked and found right: the sculptor's own matrices against three.js's for all six rotation orders over 12,000 random cases (largest difference 1.1 × 10−15); all 34 busts sculpted without an error; the busts' saving, loading and the Journal page; the wildlife changes; the new science objectives.

Changed after the review, and checked by the tests below rather than by the reviewer: the sun rays added to the warm-up; the tundra told by the ground round you (it went by the one patch underfoot, so most of the Caribou Tundra sounded like a meadow); the shore made louder (a breaking wave now carries at full loudness to 40 m, where it faded from 6 m like a small sound, and the sea's wash is about twice as loud); and two fixes to the test tools (no pointer lock, see Tests, and a page reload given the same time limit as the first load).

sections.title: What this report cannot show
sections.html:
• No real iPhone. Everything was tested in a desktop browser that imitates a phone. Safari on a real iPhone may still behave differently, above all in how long Preparing the view takes and in whether its Metal drawing finishes every shader during the warm-up draw.
  • No frame rate. The test browser draws in software, thousands of times slower than a phone's graphics chip, so the timings leave the pixels out. The draw calls and triangles are the solid numbers; how smooth it feels can only be judged on the phone.
  • The recordings were measured, not listened to. Their loudness, peaks, frequency bands and what was sounding were checked, and a bird or a footstep shows as the rise in the mids and highs it should. Whether each one sounds natural is for your ears.
  • The busts are likenesses from a description, not portraits. Each has its own sex, age, hair, beard, glasses and clothes of their time, but no sculpted features from a photograph: at the size of a small bust they read as their type, and the plaque says who it is.
  • The sources were read through search results. The environment's network rules turned away every command-line download, from every host, so each fact was checked in the search results of the pages listed below, not in the full pages. To allow the downloads, open the cloud environment menu in the session's title bar, choose Edit, and under Network access pick a broader level, or Custom with the hosts added under Allowed domains. The steps are in the cloud environments documentation.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
The conclusion is that the three new requests are done: the environment's sound is rebuilt, 34 busts of scientists stand where their work belongs, and the stalls this round could find are gone without changing the picture. These would change it:

  • It still lags on your iPhone. Then what remains is something the software test browser cannot show: the graphics chip's own time for the pixels (shadows, reflections, grass, the finish). A recording from Safari's Web Inspector on a Mac with the phone connected (Timelines, Rendering Frames) would show whether the long frames are the processor's or the graphics chip's. If the graphics chip's, the next steps (the shadow map's size, the grass's density on High) change the picture a little, so I would ask you first.
  • It stops the first time you see something. Then something escaped the warm-up, a material made later in play. Where you were and what had just come into view would pin it down.
  • Preparing the view takes too long on your phone. The warm-up can be split: what is round you first, the rest in the first seconds of play, out of sight.
  • The sound is too busy, too quiet or too loud somewhere. Each bed, each bird and each event has one level and one rate, quick to tune. Where you were, the hour and the weather are enough.
  • A bust stands somewhere odd (half in a bush, on a slope, in the way). Its spot can be moved, or the rules for a spot tightened.
  • A fact on a plaque is wrong. Each plaque is a few lines in one file, quick to correct.
